cells.tense: You sit here with the pen, and what matters arrives before you can give a reason.
cells.act: build the smallest structure that holds it
cells.ask: After your next real conversation, set down five words on paper for the thing you noticed. Not advice, not a plan. Leave the note where you'll find it and read it back later.
cells.core:
You sit with someone and things line up without you arranging them. Partway through a conversation you can feel where it needs to go, and you don't have to argue for it — it holds. That isn't cleverness. It's the sort that arrives before the thinking does, and in a room where two people are trying to meet, it's what steers.

Give one of those moments a shape this week. After the next real conversation, put the thing you noticed on paper — five words will do. No plan, no advice for anyone, nothing to defend. The smallness is the point; it costs no energy you'd have to find. Read it back later and you'll see your own hand in what you caught before you'd explained it.
cells.sheetLine: What a room needs arrives before you can explain it.
cells.verb: knowing what to attend to before you can say why
cells.place: in the room where what you feel with someone and what you know meet

cells.tense: You will have read the room so thoroughly that the first clear impression is buried under everything gathered around it.
cells.act: pick the one you would be sorriest to lose
cells.ask: Look at what you've been gathering to be sure. Choose the single thread that would sting most to drop, and stop feeding it. Nothing to throw away — just leave it. No clock on it.
cells.core:
There's a version of this where the reading gets buried. You feel the room, you feel the person, and then you go collecting — one more sign, one more angle, one more scrap of support — until the first clear thing is somewhere under the pile. The pile feels like care. From the other chair it looks like you've stopped trusting what you saw.

Choose the one thread you'd mind losing most — a person, a question, a decision — and go quiet on the others. Set the collecting down. What you noticed first either holds when nothing is propping it up or it doesn't, and you learn more from finding out than from leaning one more thing against it. No performing, no defending. Just less noise.

cells.tense: You stood at that door a while back, and some part of you is still waiting there for a sign.
cells.act: move through the fog without demanding the map
cells.ask: Name one question you've been circling. Don't try to answer it. Find the next small thing to do and do that one thing, then stop and take stock of where you actually are.
cells.core:
There's a kind of standing that feels like thinking but isn't. You've been waiting to be sure, waiting for someone to say out loud what you half-suspected, and the waiting has run long enough that you've started to treat your own read as unreliable. A step taken in dim light is still a step.

Name one question you've been circling. Don't solve it. Find the next small thing to do and do that one thing — not the whole road, just the part you can see. Then stop and take stock of where you actually are. The ground under you is likely firmer than the waiting has made it feel. It usually is.
cells.sheetLine: You're waiting for a sign to trust what you saw.
cells.verb: knowing what to attend to before you can say why

cells.tense: You're making the call already, and the room where you made it doesn't carry your name anywhere.
cells.act: give back what is owed, and take what is yours
cells.ask: Take one recent decision you called luck or a hunch. Put a sentence on paper about what you actually picked up on before you acted. Keep it where you'll find it. Nobody has to read it.
cells.core:
You make good calls and put them down as accident. The read was there — you caught what was shifting in the conversation, in the choice, in the person — and then you filed it under mood and kept moving. It happened. But you didn't put your name to it, so it doesn't count as yours.

Take one recent decision you called random and set down a sentence about what you picked up on before you acted. That's all. Nobody has to read it. The sentence isn't a confession — it's a receipt. Noticing that you were the one who called it is how the next accurate read becomes something you can use on purpose.
